a1.said: Last time, we split Snake in two. Game holds the rules, with no three p p.

a2.said: Snake View draws the game in 3D. Only the view uses three p p.

a3.said: Today, three more pieces: who plays, how the game tells others what happened, and a second game.

c1.said: Who plays the game? It could be you, on the arrow keys. Or it could be the computer.

c2.said: Every step, the game loop asks one question: which way now?

c3.said: Anything that can answer that question can play. In C plus plus, we write the question down as an interface.

c4.said: The keyboard player answers with the keys you pressed. The computer player looks at the board, and picks.

c5.said: Press tab, and the computer takes over. The loop can't tell the difference.

c6.said: Here, inheritance fits. The computer player is a kind of Controller.

v1.said: When the snake eats, the game says so, to anyone who listens.

v2.said: The view listens, and pops a ring. The game doesn't know who listens, or what they do.

r1.said: Game is a class. A class is a blueprint, and you can build as many objects from it as you like.

r2.said: So a second game is just a second object, with its own view and its own player.

r3.said: Two computer players, side by side. Nothing was copied.

z1.said: Game holds the rules. Players pick the moves. Views draw what happened.

z2.said: Keep three p p at the edge, and the middle of your program stays simple, and easy to test.
